title: Rehoboam Obeys, Fortifies Judah, and Gains the Faithful
summary: Rehoboam gathers an army to win back the northern tribes, but the prophet Shemaiah tells him not to fight his brothers, and he obeys. He fortifies a ring of cities across Judah, and priests, Levites, and faithful Israelites from the north move south because Jeroboam has set up his own priests and idols. The chapter closes with Rehoboam's large family and his choice of Abijah as heir.
story: Chapter 10 told how the united kingdom of David and Solomon split in two. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, refused to lighten the heavy labor his father had imposed, and the ten northern tribes made Jeroboam their king. From here to the end of the book, Chronicles follows only the southern kingdom of Judah, with its capital in Jerusalem and its temple and its line of David's sons. This chapter shows the first years of that smaller kingdom going surprisingly well. Rehoboam listens to a prophet, builds defenses, and receives a stream of people from the north who want to worship the LORD at his temple. The good years are real but brief. The chapter ends on a note of three years, and chapter 12 will say what happened when they were over.
historical:
Rehoboam reigned in Jerusalem for seventeen years, commonly dated to about 931 to 913 BC, though scholars differ by a few years in reconstructing the chronology of the kings. The parallel account in 1 Kings 12 records Shemaiah's word stopping the war, but the fortress list of verses 5 to 12 and the migration of priests and Levites in verses 13 to 17 appear only in Chronicles. Chronicles itself was written much later, most likely in the Persian period (roughly the late fifth or fourth century BC), for Jews back in the land after the Babylonian exile, and its writer (often called the Chronicler) drew on Samuel and Kings as well as other sources he names.

The fifteen fortified cities form a defensive screen along Judah's eastern, southern, and western approaches: Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa in the hill country; Beth-zur, Hebron, Ziph, and Adoraim to the south; Soco, Adullam, Mareshah, Lachish, Azekah, and Gath along the western foothills called the Shephelah. The northern border with Israel is conspicuously not fortified. Scholars debate whether the list reflects Rehoboam's reign as the text says or partly reflects later building, and some connect it with the Egyptian threat that arrives in chapter 12. Lachish in particular was one of Judah's major fortress cities, and its excavated remains show heavy fortification during the monarchy.
cultural:
Priests and Levites in Israel did not farm tribal land of their own. They lived in assigned towns with surrounding pasturelands (Numbers 35) and served at the sanctuary. When Jeroboam set up his own shrines at Dan and Bethel with golden calves and appointed priests who were not from the tribe of Levi (1 Kings 12:28-31), the Levites living in the north lost their calling. Leaving their pasturelands meant leaving their livelihood. The Chronicler adds to the calves a mention of goat demons, a term the law also uses in Leviticus 17:7 for the false objects of sacrifice in the wilderness, which marks Jeroboam's worship as a return to what Israel had been warned against.

The list of wives and children reflects royal practice in the ancient Near East, where marriages built alliances and many sons secured a dynasty. Rehoboam's wives are both descendants of David's family, and his favored wife Maacah is called the daughter of Absalom, David's rebel son. Sending sons out to govern fortified cities, well provisioned and married, kept them busy and loyal, and it spread royal authority across the land. The Chronicler calls this wise, even as the size of the harem recalls the multiplication of wives that Deuteronomy 17:17 warned kings against.
literary: The chapter has three panels: obedience (verses 1 to 4), strength (verses 5 to 17), and family (verses 18 to 23). The key verb of the middle panel is strengthen, which occurs at its start, in the fortifying of the cities, and at its end, where the faithful migrants strengthened the kingdom. The Chronicler thus places religious faithfulness alongside military preparation as the real source of Judah's security. The phrase "set their hearts to seek the LORD" in verse 16 introduces one of the book's central ideas, and the summary in verse 17, that they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon, prepares the reader for the turn in the next chapter.

outline.t: Shemaiah forbids war against the northern tribes, and Rehoboam obeys
Rehoboam fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin
Priests, Levites, and faithful Israelites move south
Rehoboam's wives, children, and chosen heir

doctrines.note: The word of the LORD through Shemaiah overrules a king's military plan, and the king listens. In Chronicles, prophets speak for God to kings, and a king's response to that word shapes the fortunes of the whole nation.

When the north turned to rival worship, those who wanted to seek the LORD crossed a political border to worship where God had placed his name. The true people of God is defined here by worship, not only by tribe or kingdom.
Jeroboam's priests, high places, goat demons, and calves are presented as a rejection of the LORD's appointed priesthood. Worship designed for political convenience is still false worship.

words.note: Baqash, to seek. The Chronicler uses two verbs for seeking (this one and darash) as a summary of true religion: to seek the LORD is to turn toward him in worship, prayer, and obedience. Here it describes northerners who set their hearts to seek the LORD and moved to Jerusalem to do it. The theme will return in nearly every reign that follows.

Chazaq, to be strong or to strengthen. The word describes Rehoboam strengthening his fortresses and, in related forms, recurs through the next chapters. Chronicles uses it with a double edge: strength can be God's gift to the faithful, or the point at which a king stops depending on God, as chapter 12:1 will show.

Sa'ir, literally a hairy one or goat, used here for goat demons or goat idols. The same word appears in Leviticus 17:7 for objects of illicit sacrifice. The Chronicler's addition of this word paints Jeroboam's worship in the darkest terms available.

christ: The Levites who left their homes and possessions to stand with the temple and the house of David picture a costly loyalty that the New Testament also describes. Jesus said that those who leave houses, family, or fields for his sake will receive far more (Mark 10:29-30). More directly, the chapter's concern with the true place of worship and the true line of David points ahead. The Chronicler's readers had a temple but no Davidic king on the throne, and the hope that a son of David would reign again stands behind the whole book. The New Testament presents Jesus as that son of David and as the one in whom God's people now gather to worship, so that worship is no longer tied to one city (John 4:21-24). The link here is thematic rather than a prediction.

hard.q: Why does the Chronicler call Rehoboam wise for his marriages and household when the law warned kings against many wives?
hard.a: Verse 23 praises Rehoboam's wise dispersal of his sons, not the number of his wives, and the word wise there refers to political shrewdness. The Chronicler reports eighteen wives and sixty concubines without comment, and readers who knew Deuteronomy 17:17 and the story of Solomon's wives (1 Kings 11) would draw their own conclusions. Some interpreters think the Chronicler counts large families as a sign of blessing during the king's faithful years, as he does with other kings. Others think the list is quietly ominous, since the next verse reports that Rehoboam abandoned the law once he was strong. Both readings take the text seriously, and the Chronicler leaves the tension for the reader to feel.

questions: Rehoboam gave up a war he wanted because a prophet told him to. What would it cost you to let God's word overrule a plan you have already set in motion?
The Levites left land and income to keep worshiping rightly. What have faithful people you know given up in order to stay true to God?
The chapter pairs fortresses with faithfulness as sources of strength. Which do you tend to rely on more when you feel threatened?
